title: Runtime Options: Restart Policies, Limits, and File Copying
intro: The flags you pass to 'docker run' decide how a container behaves when it crashes, how much of the host it's allowed to consume, and whether it cleans up after itself.

steps.prompt: Run a one-off container that deletes itself automatically when it exits — useful for quick throwaway commands.
steps.explanation: --rm removes the container as soon as it exits, so it never shows up in 'docker ps -a' afterward.
steps.why: Without --rm, every one-off 'docker run' leaves a stopped container behind forever — exactly the accumulation that fills up disks over months (see docker-incident-003). --rm is the right default for anything you don't intend to restart.

steps.prompt: Run 'web' so Docker restarts it automatically if it crashes, but NOT if you stop it on purpose.
steps.explanation: unless-stopped restarts on crashes and on daemon/host reboot, but respects a deliberate 'docker stop'.
steps.why: '--restart=always' also restarts on crashes, but will bring a container you manually stopped back to life after a Docker daemon restart — surprising if you stopped it on purpose. 'on-failure' only restarts on non-zero exits. unless-stopped is usually the least surprising choice for a long-running service.

steps.prompt: Run a container capped at 512MB of memory and 1.5 CPUs.
steps.explanation: Without limits, one misbehaving container can consume the entire host's memory and starve everything else on it.
steps.why: This is the Docker equivalent of Kubernetes' resources.limits — and the same trade-off applies: hitting a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed (exit code 137, see docker-tutorial-007), which is a better failure than taking down the whole host, but means the limit has to be set with real headroom above normal usage.

steps.prompt: Copy the app's log file out of the running 'web' container to your current directory.
steps.explanation: docker cp works in either direction, and works even on stopped containers — handy for pulling evidence out of a crashed container before removing it.
steps.why: You could exec in and cat the file, but that only gets it onto your screen, not onto your disk for grep/sharing — and exec doesn't work at all on a stopped container, while cp still does.

steps.prompt: Before starting a Compose stack, validate and print the fully resolved compose config (with env vars substituted) to catch mistakes.
steps.fake_output:
services:
  web:
    image: myapp:v2
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://db:5432/app
    ports:
    - 8080:3000
steps.explanation: This prints exactly what Compose will actually use after merging override files and substituting ${VARIABLES} from your .env file.
steps.why: A typo'd variable name in docker-compose.yml silently becomes an empty string at runtime — 'compose config' shows you the resolved values BEFORE anything starts, instead of discovering the problem from a confusing app error afterward.

steps.prompt: Open a shell inside the running 'web' service of your Compose stack.
steps.explanation: Same as docker exec, but addressed by Compose service name instead of container id.
steps.why: Compose container names get auto-generated prefixes/suffixes (like myapp-web-1) — using the service name via 'compose exec' means you never need to look those up.
